::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
What do you learn first, and what does your group standardise on? Both are
expensive to reverse — the first costs you a year, the second costs an
organisation several.
:::

## 1. The rule that matters more than the choice

**Learn one language until you never fight it, then learn the second in a
fortnight.**

Almost every beginner does the opposite: a little R, a little Python, some
NONMEM syntax, a Julia tutorial. The result is four tools at the level where
each one still costs you an hour a day in friction. Fluency in one is worth more
than familiarity with four, because fluency is what lets you think about the
model instead of the syntax.

Which one you pick first matters far less than people argue. The differences
between competent modelers using different stacks are invisible in the output.

## 2. Languages

| | **R** | **Python** | **Julia** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Position in the field | The lingua franca | Growing fast, dominant in adjacent teams | Small but serious, concentrated around Pumas and SciML |
| Ecosystem | Deepest pharmacometrics tooling anywhere | Best general data, ML and engineering libraries | Excellent numerics and differential equations |
| Estimation | `nlmixr2`, plus interfaces to everything | Weakest link — few mature NLME options | `Pumas` is a first-class NLME engine |
| Simulation | `mrgsolve`, `rxode2` — both excellent | `scipy`, and thinner PK-specific tooling | `DifferentialEquations.jl`, best-in-class |
| Reporting | Quarto, `ggplot2`, `xpose` | Quarto, `matplotlib`, `plotly` | Quarto, `Makie` |
| Hiring reality | Expected in most pharmacometrics roles | Expected in data-science-adjacent roles | Rarely required, sometimes a differentiator |
| Learning cost | Idiosyncratic but well-documented | Gentlest for a general programmer | Steepest; small community to ask |

**A defensible default:** R first if you are aiming at pharmacometrics roles,
Python first if you are crossing over from data science and want your existing
fluency to keep paying. Julia if you already know why you want it.

This site writes both R and Python for every runnable lesson, so the choice
does not gate you here. It will gate you at work.

## 3. Estimation engines

This is where the money and the politics are.

| | **NONMEM** | **nlmixr2** | **Monolix** | **Pumas** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Licence | Commercial | Open source | Commercial | Commercial; free academic licence |
| Language | Its own control-stream syntax | R | GUI plus MLXTRAN | Julia |
| Regulatory familiarity | The reference standard; decades of submissions | Growing, increasingly seen in submissions | Well established, widely accepted | Newer; acceptance growing |
| Estimation | FOCE-I, SAEM, importance sampling | FOCE-I, SAEM, and more | SAEM (its strength) | FOCE-I, SAEM, plus modern optimisers |
| Learning curve | Steep, unusual, unforgiving | Moderate if you know R | Gentlest — the GUI genuinely helps | Moderate if you know Julia |
| Speed | Fast, mature | Competitive | Fast, especially SAEM | Fast; strong parallelism |
| Best for | Anything that will be filed | Learning, and open reproducible work | Complex models, teams that value the interface | Teams already in Julia; heavy simulation |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**If you are learning alone, start with `nlmixr2`.** It costs nothing, it runs
in the language you are already learning, its syntax is readable, and the
concepts transfer directly. Learn NONMEM when a job requires it — and one will,
because the installed base in regulatory submissions is enormous and will remain
so for a long time.

Learning NONMEM control-stream syntax *before* understanding mixed-effects
models is the single most common way people waste six months.
:::

## 4. Simulation and mechanistic tools

| Tool | What it is for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `mrgsolve` (R) | Fast ODE simulation from a compact model spec | The standard for clinical trial simulation in R |
| `rxode2` (R) | Simulation engine underneath `nlmixr2` | Same model syntax as the estimation step — a real advantage |
| `DifferentialEquations.jl` | General, very fast ODE/SDE/DDE solving | Best numerics available in any of the three languages |
| `scipy.integrate` | General-purpose Python solving | Fine for teaching and moderate problems; slower at population scale |
| **PK-Sim / MoBi** | Whole-body PBPK, open source | The Open Systems Pharmacology suite — free, credible, used in submissions |
| **Simcyp / GastroPlus** | Commercial PBPK platforms | Extensive built-in populations and *in vitro* databases; expensive |
| **Stan / Torsten** | Full Bayesian PK/PD | Torsten adds PK/PD event handling to Stan; the serious Bayesian route |

## 5. What to standardise on, if you are choosing for a group

Different question, different answer. For an individual, optimise for learning
speed. For a group, optimise for the things that cost you when they go wrong:

1. **Reproducibility over preference.** A stack everyone can install and re-run
   in three years beats a faster one that only two people can drive.
2. **Regulatory familiarity where it counts.** The filing analysis is not the
   place to be the first submission a reviewer has seen in your tool.
3. **Hiring pool.** You will replace people. A stack nobody knows is a
   recruitment tax you pay forever.
4. **One escape hatch, not five.** Being able to move a model between two tools
   is valuable insurance. Maintaining it in four is a cost with no benefit.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — the tool as identity
Tool arguments in this field are unusually heated, and they are almost never
about the tools. People defend the thing they invested years in. It reliably
produces two costly behaviours: reaching for the familiar tool when the question
suits another one, and dismissing a colleague's analysis on the basis of what it
was run in.

The countermeasure is concrete: at least once, fit the same model in two engines
and compare the estimates. It is the fastest cure for tool mysticism, it is a
genuinely useful validation habit, and it is why the `Rosetta` panels exist on
this site.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. You have six months and want a pharmacometrics job. What do you learn?
R to fluency, `nlmixr2` for estimation, `mrgsolve` or `rxode2` for simulation,
Quarto for reporting, git for everything. Not Python as well, not Julia, not
NONMEM syntax before the concepts. Depth in the standard stack, plus one
finished public analysis, beats breadth every time at the hiring stage.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your group runs NONMEM. Is learning nlmixr2 wasted effort?
No, and for a specific reason: reproducing a NONMEM result in an open engine is
one of the strongest validation checks available, and it costs a day. It also
gives you something you can share publicly, teach with, and run without a
licence server. The waste would be maintaining both as production pipelines.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. When is Python the wrong choice for an estimation task?
When you need mature NLME estimation with the diagnostics and regulatory
familiarity the field expects. Python's general ecosystem is superb and its
NLME ecosystem is thin — that gap is the honest reason R still dominates
pharmacometrics despite Python winning nearly everywhere else. Python remains a
fine choice for simulation, data assembly, ML work and reporting.
:::

## Going further

- **Next:** [S0-05 · Git for modelers](../s0-05-git-for-modelers/).
- **Reference:** each tool's own tutorial, written by its authors and mostly
  free: Bauer RJ on NONMEM, part I ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12404))
  and part II ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12422)); Wang W et al. on
  RxODE ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12052)); Elmokadem A, Riggs MM,
  Baron KT on mrgsolve for PBPK and QSP
  ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.12467)); Keizer RJ, Karlsson MO, Hooker A
  on the Pirana/PsN/Xpose workbench ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/psp.2013.24)).
  Also the Open Systems Pharmacology suite for PBPK, and Torsten's user guide for
  Bayesian PK/PD.

*Seen in the wild:* a team spent four months porting a model from one platform to
another for reasons that were entirely about a licence renewal. The port
introduced two parameterisation differences that took another six weeks to
reconcile. The lesson is not that porting is bad — it is that a port is a
project with a schedule, not an afternoon.
